feedback: If the learner says one muscle pushes the arm straight again: muscles only pull — press your palm down on the table to straighten the arm, and feel that the biceps softens while the triceps on the other side tightens and pulls the arm straight.
If they think the relaxing muscle pushes the limb back: a relaxing muscle just softens and lets go; it is the OPPOSITE muscle contracting that moves the bone back.
Prompt: which side tightens when you bend? Which side tightens when you straighten? That is your pair.
activities.intendedInsight: A contracting muscle shortens and pulls a bone; it cannot push. To move the bone back the other way, a second muscle on the opposite side must contract and pull — this is the antagonistic pair. 'Contract' and 'relax' are concrete opposites you can feel.
learnerActions: Place your free hand on the front of your upper arm (the biceps), then bend your elbow to raise your forearm — notice the biceps bunch up, getting shorter and harder.

Keeping your hand there, straighten your arm by pressing your palm firmly down on a table top (or pushing against a wall) — feel the biceps soften. (If you just let your forearm lower slowly on its own, gravity does most of the work and the biceps stays partly tight to control the fall, so the change is harder to feel.)

Now feel the back of your upper arm (the triceps) and press down on the table again to straighten the arm: notice that the back (triceps) tightens while the front relaxes. Straightening against a push like this is what makes the triceps work hard enough to feel.
Say out loud each time: 'Which muscle is pulling now, and which has relaxed?'
activities.title: Feel the pair on your own arm

feedback: If the learner claims all muscles are voluntary / that you could stop your heart by deciding to: you can choose to bend your arm, but your heart keeps beating whether you think about it or not — it is involuntary.
If they think the heart is not a muscle: the heart is a muscle, but an involuntary one that works automatically all the time.
Link back: the muscles that move food through digestion also work by themselves, without you choosing.
activities.intendedInsight: Voluntary muscles are under conscious control; involuntary muscles (the heart, digestive muscles) work automatically without any decision. The heart IS a muscle — an involuntary one that never stops working, all your life.
learnerActions: For each muscle, ask: 'Do I choose to move it, or does it work on its own?'
Sort examples: arm muscles and leg muscles (voluntary — you decide), the heart and the muscles that squeeze food along the digestive system (involuntary — automatic).
Try the test: you can decide to bend your arm — but try to decide to stop your heart from beating. You cannot. That shows it is involuntary.
Name at least one involuntary muscle from memory (heart; digestive/gut muscles) and explain why automatic control is useful (it keeps you alive without you having to think about it).
activities.title: Voluntary or involuntary? Sort the muscles

feedback: For contract/relax questions, reason from which muscle is pulling for that movement — do not guess by size (the bigger muscle is not automatically the straightener).
If an answer attributes the return movement to a muscle pushing, re-state: muscles only pull; the partner pulls the other way.
Reward transfer: correctly applying 'pairs because muscles only pull' to a new joint shows real understanding.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates that muscles pull in opposing pairs and that voluntary and involuntary muscles differ, including applying the reasoning to a new joint or muscle.
learnerActions: For a given movement (e.g. bending the arm), say which muscle contracts and which relaxes.
Categorise a list of muscles as voluntary or involuntary.
Match each action (bend arm / straighten arm) to the muscle that pulls to produce it.
Transfer: explain how a pair would work at another joint, or name another involuntary muscle.
activities.title: Consolidation check
